title: Vertical chiral emission from an intrinsically achiral metasurface enabled with anisotropic continuum

paper_content.abstract: Manipulating emission polarization is crucial for advanced applications such as polarized fluorescence and lasing, thermal radiation control, stereochemistry and spintronics. Existing approaches for generating circularly polarized emission primarily rely on nanostructures with true chirality, where the far-field polarization at the Γ point is believed to require out-of-plane symmetry breaking. This raises a question: can an intrinsically achiral metasurface that preserves out-of-plane symmetry generate chiral emission? Here, we introduce the concept of anisotropic continuum, defined as a continuum state exhibiting distinct responses for orthogonal polarizations of incidence, as a new degree of freedom for intrinsically achiral metasurfaces. In such metasurfaces, chiral emission arises from manipulating the anisotropic continuum together with the metasurface’s in-plane perturbations. Degrees of circular polarization of 0.83 for upward emission and −0.9 for downward emission are achieved experimentally by integrating the fabricated silicon metasurface with fluorescent organic dyes. Our findings not only address a long-standing gap in the understanding of structural chirality, but also open new opportunities for high-performance applications in polarized fluorescence and thermal emission.
paper_content.introduction:
Electromagnetic chirality refers to the phenomenon in which an object interacts differently with right and left circularly polarized (RCP/LCP) light1–4, a property commonly observed in natural materials with three-dimensional asymmetric structures. This chiral behavior gives rise to a distinct chiroptical response, which can be characterized by circular dichroism (CD) or optical rotation5. While natural materials have been used to generate chiral emission, their low chirality and limited tunability constrain practical applications6,7. Metasurfaces, however, offer a powerful platform to enhance and control chiral emission, enabling new opportunities in polarized emission8–13, chirality tuning14,15, chiral sensing16,17, and photodetection18,19.

Recent advances in chiral metasurfaces and their ability to generate chiral emission have been driven by the incorporation of non-local resonances, especially bound states in the continuum (BIC)20–29 and guided modes30. In such systems, light remains confined within the metasurface while coexisting with a continuum of electromagnetic waves. Typically, intrinsic chirality in metasurfaces, characterized by chiroptical responses at the Γ point, is achieved in geometrically chiral structures through symmetry breaking across all mirror planes6,31–34. To break the out-of-plane mirror symmetry (σz symmetry) and achieve chiral quasi-BIC, various methods have been employed, including slant-etching9,24, grayscale lithography10,25 and bi-layer design35. In these structures, chiral emission arises when the quasi-BIC aligns with a high-transmission background. With mirror symmetry breaking in all planes, chiral emission occurs when near-unity CD is observed (indicated in the left panel of Fig. 1a)24,28. Here, chiral emission refers to a radiative process in which the far-field degree of circular polarization (DCP=(IR − IL)/(IR + IL)) approaches unity. Planar chiral metasurfaces represent another route, where near-unity CD29,36,37 at normal incidence has also been reported. However, these designs primarily focus on transmission properties, and their potential for controlling emission remains largely unexplored (see Supplementary Section 1). Moreover, recent studies have revealed that a large CD in transmission does not necessarily correspond to chiral emission24, highlighting a gap in understanding the emission mechanism of planar chiral systems. In our earlier work, chiral emission was observed in the presence of a dielectric substrate that perturbed σz symmetry12. Conventionally, σz-symmetric metasurfaces are believed to support only extrinsic chiral emission away from the Γ point, typically enabled by breaking in-plane inversion symmetry38–41. The far-field polarization at the Γ point, by contrast, is generally considered nearly linear due to the absence of geometric chirality21,24,28,42. An interesting question arises: can a metasurface with σz symmetry, which is intrinsically achiral, generate circular or even arbitrary polarization at the Γ point? Our answer is yes.

Here, we demonstrate theoretically and experimentally that breaking σz symmetry is not required to generate chiral emission at the Γ point, using a vertically etched silicon metasurface embedded in a uniform environment (right panel of Fig. 1a). An additional degree of freedom is introduced by leveraging anisotropic continuum, characterized by distinct responses for orthogonal polarizations in the continuum, e.g., x-polarized and y-polarized light. The term continuum refers to a range of states that are closely connected and form a smooth, uninterrupted spectrum43. In metasurfaces, the continuum is characterized by a slowly-varying reflection/transmission spectrum, induced by Fabry-Perot resonances44, Mie resonances45, high-contrast grating effects46, and other mechanisms. We show that when a bound mode is embedded within an anisotropic continuum, in-plane perturbations can induce radiative coupling. This leads to chiral emission within a specific continuum, where the radiated polarization exhibits opposite chirality in the upward and downward directions. While ultrahigh-Q modes in metasurfaces, such as quasi-BIC47,48 and leaky guided modes30,49,50, have been extensively studied and widely applied in photonics, the specific influence of the continuum on emission polarization remains largely unexplored. Related work has examined its effect on linearly polarized emission51, whereas its contribution to chiral emission remains an open and critical question. Understanding the role of these states could open new avenues for designing metasurfaces with customized polarization properties.
paper_content.results:
To show the importance of anisotropic continuum in realizing chiral emission in σz-symmetric metasurfaces, we decompose the far-field polarization of a resonant mode in the σz-symmetric metasurface into Cartesian components |Ex|eiθx and |Ey|eiθy. It is determined by two critical parameters: (i) the phase difference between the x- and y-components Ex and Ey, expressed as φ=θy − θx=arg(Ey/Ex) and (ii) the magnitude ratio of Ex and Ey, denoted as η=|Ey|/|Ex|. We start with a structure that exhibits no polarization conversion in either transmission or reflection between the x- and y-polarized channels to simplify the analysis. For a discrete localized state, the phase difference φ can be expressed in terms of background reflection and transmission coefficients (rx, ry, tx, ty) as follows (Supplementary Section 2)44,52

φ = arg(ry + αz ty) − arg(rx + αz tx) + nπ, (1)

where n is an integer and αz=±1 is a parity number. This equation establishes a connection between the eigenstate far-field polarization and the scattering coefficients of the continuum.

The relation between the eigenstate phase difference φ and the continuum transmission spectra in a σz-symmetric structure is conceptually demonstrated in Fig. 1b. For metasurfaces with a transmissive background or anisotropic continuum (left panels of Fig. 1b), φ is always zero and the vertically radiated polarization remains linearly polarized. For instance, metasurfaces with the unit cell composed of cylinders or circular apertures are unable to generate an arbitrary phase difference φ as they inherently satisfy arg(ry + αz ty)=arg(rx + αz tx). In contrast, a nonzero phase difference between the x- and y-components of the radiated electric field can be generated with the assistance of the anisotropic continuum (right panels of Fig. 1b). To achieve chiral emission, φ=π/2 should be satisfied first. This requires that the metasurface should generally be geometrically anisotropic in a certain direction.

Due to the presence of anisotropic continuum, the transmission and reflection spectra of σz-symmetric metasurfaces exhibit unique features compared with σz-asymmetric ones. As shown in Fig. 1c, under the condition of DCP=1, RCP incidence excites a strong resonance; however, its transmission remains identical to the non-resonant direct transmission under LCP incidence, due to destructive interference with the background (Supplementary Section 3). Consequently, the transmission CD at the Γ point ideally vanishes when the resonant and background scatterings are exactly out of phase.

We consider a σz-symmetric dielectric metasurface, schematically shown in Fig. 1d. The unit cell consists of a silicon dimer embedded in a silica environment, preserving σz symmetry regardless of in-plane variations. This adopted structure follows our earlier work to isolate and emphasize the role of out-of-plane mirror symmetry12. The phase difference φ of the structure is governed by anisotropic continuum modulation, while the ratio η=|Ey|/|Ex| is influenced by in-plane perturbations. Initially, with α=0 and δt=0, no symmetry breaking occurs, and the introduction of the continuum results in φ=π/2. In this condition, the bound mode is embedded in the continuum, allowing coupling to x-polarized waves. Further introducing nonzero α induces simultaneous non-zero |Ex| and |Ey|, producing circular polarization. In this step, breaking the in-plane mirror symmetry to make the structure “2D-chiral” is essential for generating both |Ex| and |Ey|, as the in-plane mirror symmetry guarantees linear polarization. Figure 1e provides a clearer illustration of the role of the anisotropic continuum. The polarization of the far-field radiation can be fully described by a set of Stokes parameters: S1=(|Ex|2−|Ey|2)/(|Ex|2+|Ey|2), S2=2|Ex||Ey|cosφ/(|Ex|2+|Ey|2), S3=2|Ex||Ey|sinφ/(|Ex|2+|Ey|2). Once φ is fixed, the Stokes parameters trace an arc on the Poincare sphere connecting two opposite points on the S1 axis as |Ex| and |Ey| vary. In this case, the phase difference φ is the angle between the arc and the equator, while |Ey|/|Ex| controls the distance between the observed point and the pole along the S1 axis. Without the contribution of anisotropic continuum, radiative modes induced by in-plane symmetry breaking trace a line along the equator of the Poincare sphere (gray line in Fig. 1e). When anisotropic continuum is introduced, this line is lifted toward either the northern or southern hemisphere. Under specific structural parameters, the trajectory intersects the pole, marked by a red star. This evolution is further depicted in the right panel of Fig. 1e, highlighting the changes in the radiated polarization as the structural parameters vary.

To demonstrate control over the phase difference φ, we select an unperturbed metasurface with α=0 and δt=0, and then vary the pillar length L. This variation induces anisotropy of the background response, which results in nontrivial values of φ according to Eq. (1). Note also that the phase difference φ depends on the relative positions between the bound mode and the broad transmission dip of Ty. The variation of φ with L is shown in Fig. 2a, where φ decreases with increasing L and reaches φ=π/2 when L=190 nm. The corresponding transmission spectra Tx and Ty for L=190 nm are shown in the inset of Fig. 2a, with the position of the bound mode marked as a red star. Under this condition, further modulation of the asymmetric parameters α and δt transforms the bound mode into a bright mode that radiates into the far-field. The far-field polarization distribution in k-space is shown on the right side of Fig. 2b, revealing a C point at the Γ point.

A silicon metasurface with α=0.09 and δt=11 nm is fabricated on a silica substrate to experimentally verify our theoretical predictions. The metasurface is subsequently covered with a 50 μm layer of PMMA to achieve refractive index matching with the silica substrate24 (so that the silicon metasurface is symmetrical along the vertical direction) and to minimize the impact of Fabry-Perot resonance on the spectrum. Figure 2c presents the overall scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of the silicon metasurface together with a schematic illustration in the x-z plane, revealing vertically etched structures that preserve the out-of-plane mirror symmetry. Angle-resolved transmission spectra for transverse electric (TE) and transverse magnetic (TM) polarized incident light, denoted by TTE and TTM, respectively, are confirmed by simulations and experiments in Fig. 2d. Under TM-polarized incidence, only the TM mode is excited, whereas TE-polarized incidence excites TM1, TE1, and TM2 modes (note that TE/TM incidence refers to the incident polarization, while TE/TM modes refer to the eigenmodes). The TM1 mode couples to TE and TM components, residing within the broad transmission dip observed under TE incidence. The experimental results closely align with the simulations, confirming the coupling of the TM1 mode to both the x- and y-polarization components and its modulation by the continuum. While the primary discussion in the main text focuses on the TM1 mode, the TE mode also holds potential for chiral emission, as elaborated in the Supplementary Section 4.

To investigate the evolution of radiated polarization, we fabricated a series of metasurfaces with varying configurations: zero α and δt, nonzero δt only, and both nonzero α and δt. Transmission spectra of these metasurfaces were simulated (solid lines in Fig. 3), theoretically derived with TCMT (indicated by “×” in Fig. 3), and experimentally measured (indicated by “Δ” in Fig. 3) to provide insight into the continuum and bound modes. For α=0 and δt=0, the transmission spectrum Ty exhibits a broad dip between 700 nm and 900 nm, while Tx maintains high transmission (Fig. 3a). In this configuration, no bound mode is excited due to symmetry protection. The phase difference φ is calculated through Eq. (1) with αz=−1, and is depicted as a dotted gray line in the upper panel of Fig. 3a. Although a nonzero φ is generated across the wavelength range, we have |Ex|=|Ey|=0. For α=0 and δt=11 nm, the bound TM1 mode becomes leaky, experimentally resulting in a sharp transmission dip at λ=778 nm for Tx, while the line shape of Ty remains nearly unchanged (Fig. 3b). This leakage, independent of C2 symmetry breaking, indicates that the mode is a quasi-guided mode arising from band-doubling rather than a symmetry-protected BIC. For α=0.09 and δt=11 nm, the transmission spectra exhibit resonant features under both x-polarized and y-polarized light illumination. At λ=775 nm, a transmission dip appears for Tx while a transmission peak emerges for Ty, located near the broad dip of Ty (Fig. 3c). The simultaneous presence of the dip and peak signifies coupling to both x- and y-polarizations. The TCMT-fitted spectra show excellent agreement with numerical simulations, validating that the model accurately describes the key features of vertical chiral emission.

In terms of the resonant mode field distribution, the coupling behavior can be directly understood from the overlap integral between the incident field and the resonant mode: symmetry enforces zero overlap, δt alone allows coupling only to x-polarization, and the combination of δt and α yields finite overlap for both x- and y-polarizations with a phase difference close to π/2. Full derivations and supporting figures are provided in Supplementary Section 5.

The chiral emission capabilities of metasurfaces play a significant role in modulating fluorescence, laser emission and thermal radiation. Here, we further examine the fluorescence properties enabled by the σz-symmetric dielectric metasurface, with the absorption characteristics shown in Supplementary Section 6. As shown in Fig. 4a, in the case where L=190 nm, the long and short axes of the radiated polarization consistently align with the x or y axis, with only the ellipticity changing as α and δt vary. Thus, the phase difference φ remains nearly π/2 for small values of α and δt. This variation demonstrates that the phase difference φ induced by continuum scattering coefficients is robust against in-plane perturbations. Since δt and α control |Ex| and |Ey| independently, there are multiple instances where |Ey|/|Ex|=1, resulting in C points (Fig. 4b). Larger values of α and δt introduce greater symmetry breaking, which leads to lower Q-factors. In the experiment, a thin layer of IR140 organic dye is first spin-coated onto the fabricated metasurface, followed by a 50 μm PMMA coating. The sample is then excited with a 532 nm laser, and its photoluminescence (PL) characteristics are analyzed (Supplementary Section 7). The PL from the dye is strongly modulated by the TM1 mode supported by the metasurface, with its polarization determined by the eigenstate. Figure 4c displays the polarization-resolved upward PL spectra for three cases with different α values at a fixed δt of 11 nm. For α=0, the RCP and LCP components of the PL spectrum are nearly equal, indicating linearly polarized emission. As α increases, the proportion of the LCP component decreases, resulting in an increased DCP.

Figure 4d demonstrates the x-z cross sections of Ex±iEy of the eigenstate in the case of α=0.09 and δt=11 nm. The upward and downward leaky waves are RCP (red circular line) and LCP (blue circular line), both represented by Ex − iEy due to the change in direction21. The reversal of radiated circular polarization is expected, given that the structure exhibits opposite chirality when viewed from above and below. Experimentally, a prominent RCP peak is detected in the upward emission, with negligible LCP contribution, resulting in a DCP of 0.83 (upper half of Fig. 4e). Conversely, for downward emission, the LCP component dominates, yielding a DCP of −0.9 (lower half of Fig. 4e). This reversal in circular polarization confirms the absence of net chiral flux in the far field, consistent with the preserved σz symmetry. The small difference in absolute DCP between the upward and downward emissions may be attributed to the coated thin dye layer, which degrades the out-of-plane symmetry to some extent.
paper_content.methods:
Numerical simulation
All simulations are performed using COMSOL Multiphysics 5.6 “Electromagnetic Waves Frequency Domain” module. The refractive indices of silicon and surrounding materials are taken as nSi=3.9 (Supplementary Section 10) and nPMMA=nSiO2=1.45, respectively. Periodic conditions are applied in the x and y directions of the simulated unit cell, and perfectly matched layers are employed along the z direction. The far-field eigen-polarization is calculated through COMSOL Multiphysics 5.6 with MATLAB. In the calculation of continuum transmission, the incidence port is set as x/y polarization by setting the electric mode field to (1, 0, 0) or (0, 1, 0). Equation (1) is calculated through the polarization-resolved scattering coefficients obtained from ports.

Sample fabrication
A layer of 210 nm silicon is deposited on a 4-inch silica substrate through plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition and subsequently cleaved into small 1 cm × 1 cm slices. Each sample is cleaned sequentially in acetone, isopropyl alcohol, and deionized water, and then spin-coated with 270 nm electron-beam resist (PMMA 679.04). The pattern is defined by E-beam exposure (Raith 150 EBL) and developed in methyl isobutyl ketone and isopropyl alcohol. A 30 nm Al film is deposited using electron beam evaporation (Denton) as the hard mask onto the patterned resist and is lifted off by ultrasonic cleaning in acetone. The pattern is then transferred to the silicon by dry etching (Multiplex ICP STS) using C4F8 and SF6, and the residual Al is finally removed in the Al etching solution. The fabrication process of the sample is summarized in Supplementary Section 10.

Covering of IR140 and PMMA
The fabricated sample is cleaned first with acetone and isopropyl alcohol, and then baked on a hot plate at 120 °C for 10 min. The clean sample is spin-coated with a drop of 20 μL IR140 dissolved in ethanol in the following steps: starting at 500 rpm for 3 s, followed by 2000 rpm for 30 s, and lastly at 0 rpm for 3 s. The coated sample is left for stand for 5 min to evaporate the ethanol and improve the film uniformity. To form a thick PMMA layer on the metasurface, the PMMA solution is concentrated through solvent evaporation. Then, the PMMA is spin-coated on the metasurface in the following steps: starting at 500 rpm for 3 s, followed by 4000 rpm for 60 s, and lastly at 0 rpm for 3 s. A layer of 50 μm PMMA is formed by repeating this procedure five times.

Optical characterization
In the transmission measurement, the sample is fixed on a rotating sample stage (Supplementary Section 6). A white light source is turned on and the light passes through a polarizer and an aperture before being focused onto the sample by an objective lens of a low numerical aperture, in which case the incident wave can be treated as an approximate plane wave. The incident polarization is switched between x and y by rotating the polarizer. The transmission spectra for different incident angles are collected by rotating the sample stage. In the PL measurement, a 532 nm continuous-wave laser is used to stimulate IR140 organic dyes. The PL is collected by a 20× objective lens, and analyzed by a zero-order quarter-wave plate, a half-wave plate and a linear polarizer. The fast axis of the quarter-wave plate is fixed to 45° with respect to the polarizer. When the fast axis of the half-wave plate is rotated to 0°/45°, RCP/LCP light is selected.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In the submitted manuscript, the authors studied vertical chiral emission from dielectric metasurfaces that preserve out-of-plane (sigma_z) symmetry. They conducted very detailed theoretical studies on how the polarization state of radiation from an out-of-plane symmetric dielectric metasurface is influenced by anisotropic non-resonant background scattering (called scattering by 'anisotropic continuum' in the current manuscript). The authors also verified their theoretical studies by measuring chiral emission from the emitter-coated dielectric metasurface and reported very good experimental results for vertical chiral emission. The current study surely enhances a fundamental understanding of planar chiral structures and provides novel insights into chiral metasurface design. The manuscript is well written, and I think that the current study could be of great interest to the relevant research communities.
However, I see several important issues in the current manuscript. There have been several relevant studies in literature. And the merits of the out-of-plane symmetric metasurfaces for chiral emission are still not clear. Specifically, I'd like to ask the authors to clarify the following issues:
1) It was previously noted that the polarization state of radiation from a dielectric metasurface (or photonic crystal slab) is strongly constrained by the direct non-resonant scattering (or continuum scattering) process. For example, see
- arXiv:1708.02197 (2017), "Polarization state of radiation from a photonic crystal slab"
The discussions in the current manuscript seem closely related to this previous study. This article also commented that, when the direct-scattering (or continuum-scattering) coefficients are the same for the two orthogonal polarization components, the radiation from the dielectric slab should be linearly polarized.
As another example, the following paper studied how to achieve maximal planar chirality using dielectric metasurfaces. This article also noted that no chiral response can be obtained if the effective background only has an isotropic response (Section II in Supporting Information).
- Nat. Comm. (2022) 13:4111, "Planar chiral metasurfaces with maximal and tunable chiroptical response driven by bound states in the continuum"
Therefore, I think the authors should clarify the advancement and difference of the current manuscript compared to the previous studies in literature.
2) Terminology issue: The title includes the term 'non-chiral'. I suppose the authors wanted to stress that the current study considered a more ideal case for planar chiral metasurfaces that preserved out-of-plane symmetry while previous studies mostly considered structures that still involved out-of-plane symmetry breaking. However, the current study also used a chiral geometry (non-zero alpha in Figure 1a) that breaks in-plane mirror symmetry, and this type of structure has been commonly called planar 'chiral' structure in literature. Therefore, the use of the term 'non-chiral' could be very confusing. It would be great if the authors could come up with a different term.
3) In the current manuscript, the authors demonstrated vertical chiral emission from dielectric metasurfaces that preserve out-of-plane symmetry. However, similar chiral emission in the vertical direction is also expected from planar chiral metasurfaces on a substrate that break the out-plane-symmetry [e.g., when emitters are coated on the planar dielectric structures in the article above, Nat. Comm. (2022) 13:4111]. Do out-of-plane symmetric metasurfaces have 'practical merits' for chiral emission compared to other planar chiral structures?
4) In Figure 4, the authors considered asymmetric parameter ‘alpha’ up to 0.09. The chiral response (degree of circular polarization, DCP) gradually increased up to this point. Then, what happens when the alpha increases further beyond 0.09? And what is the optimal value of alpha in the current design?
5) Effect of absorption losses: In the current manuscript, I think lossless dielectric structures are assumed. But light emission from emitters (either from dye molecules or from semiconductor materials) implies that absorption should also exist at the same wavelength. Therefore, emitter-integrated dielectric metasurfaces should have some absorption losses at the emission wavelength. How do the absorption losses affect the theoretical description of vertical chiral emission in the current manuscript? Is anisotropic continuum still required for vertical chiral emission? For example, according to the current study, gammadion structures made of lossless dielectric materials cannot be used for vertical chiral emission because they are rotationally symmetric and do not support anisotropic continuum scattering. However, when emitters are integrated with such lossless dielectric metasurfaces, the entire system becomes lossy. I am wondering whether vertical chiral emission is still suppressed in this case (or it can be now achieved without anisotropic continuum).
In a similar way, I suppose that plasmonic chiral metasurfaces may behave differently for vertical chiral emission due to their intrinsic absorption losses (in addition to the absorption losses of emitters). I would be thankful if the authors clarify these issues.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors report on the design and experimental demonstration of a planar metasurface of broken in-plane symmetry, which hosts specific high quality factor photonic eigenstates emitting circularly polarized waves of opposite handedness in the vertical up and down directions. They study how such a state arises in arrays of silicon nanobar dimers subjected to weak symmetry breaking perturbations and attempt to relate the emission chirality with a birefringent background scattering (here called anisotropic continuum). Such metasurfaces are then fabricated and demonstrate that indeed, upon cladding with luminescent organic dye, the properly designed samples emit light with the degree of circular polarization (DCP) up to 0.9 in magnitude and of the opposite handedness in the opposite directions. The paper is accompanied by the Supplementary Information (SI) elaborating proposed theoretical explanations formulated in terms of the temporal coupled-mode theory (TCMT), describing the details of fabrication and optical experiments. Additional modeling clarifies the role of material parameters as well as suggests how the proposed approach can be realized using differently shaped meta-atoms.
The subject of the paper is very timely: high-purity sources of chiral light are desired for many emerging chiroptical applications. The main simulations and experimental results look solid and support the conclusion that a planar metasurface can emit circularly polarized light. However, this has already been shown in recent works published by essentially the same group!
I cannot recommend publishing in NatComm as I seriously doubt the qualitative novelty of this work.
My doubts are further strengthened by the fact that the authors avoid citing their own papers, and only briefly mention one in the SI.
As a matter of fact, practically identically designed metasurface was used in [R1] to perform exactly the same task and has reached DNC up to 0.74 of emission of a quantum dot cladding. The particular size parameters are different now to ensure a somewhat different emission wavelength. However, the metasurface design is identical to that in [R1]. Compared to [R1], the manuscript contains only more elaborate (and not always well justified) theoretical explanations and additional simulations. Note also that in another recent Ref. [R2] the authors present a similarly designed trimer metasurface performing chiral thermal emission. Therefore, I strongly doubt the novelty of the current findings.
Having stated this, I must recognize the potential importance of the theoretical framework developed in order to explain the simulated and repeatedly measured properties. As the authors will definitely look for opportunities to publish their work elsewhere, I formulate a couple of related suggestions and critical remarks:
1. Simulated (Fig 1b) and measured (Fig. 3) transmission spectra clearly resemble those generally predicted 20 years ago in Ref. [52] for a pair of non-orthogonal modes of an open lossless resonator. More recently, such modes are termed “coupled via-the-continuum” [48]. It seems much more reasonable to start with postulating the existence of two modes of the same parity rather than to presume the existence of strongly birefringent background of unknown origin. Note that I am unaware of a justified procedure of rewriting TCMT equations in order to include a state into the background. From the general viewpoint, this may severely violate the energy conservation. Presumably, Section S3 of the SI attempts to describe such a procedure, but it is hard to comprehend this section due to many undefined notations and possible typos. Please provide a detailed explanation how a state can be phenomenologically included into the background. Otherwise, one can directly follow the strategy of Ref. [52] and start with a pair of states.
2. To clarify the peculiar eigenstate interplay, it might be useful to analyze them in metasurfaces subjected to different symmetry perturbations as those used to produce Fig. 3. In particular, this could elucidate how the shape perturbations open the state coupling via the continuum. Note also that the field distributions of the states are now given only on a single tiny inset in Fig 2a. These can also clarify the states origin, their coupling and the role of symmetry breaking perturbations.
3, Finally, to prove the TCMT applicability, one usually derives the model expressions for the transmission and reflection amplitudes and shows how well they fit the simulated transmission and reflection spectra. Otherwise, the usefulness of TCMT remains elusive. Successful fitting will definitely demonstrate that all essential phenomena are adequately understood and captured by the phenomenology.
[R1] Sun, Y. et al. Enhancing Circularly Polarized Emission by a Planar Chiral Dielectric Metasurface. Advanced Optical Materials 2300197 (2023) doi:10.1002/adom.202300197.
[R2] Sun, Y., Shi, K., Hu, Z., Jin, Y. & He, S. Highly circularly polarized and coherent thermal emission based on chiral quasi bound states in the continuum. Opt. Lett. 49, 6329 (2024).

submitted to Nature Communications
We would like to sincerely thank the Editor and Reviewers for their careful
evaluation of our manuscript and their constructive comments, which have helped us
substantially improve the clarity, completeness, and scientific rigor of our work.
Considering these critical comments, we have further stated the novelty and related
advantages of our work in the areas of chiral emission, while the changes in the revised
manuscripts are marked in red. In the following, we provide a point-to-point response
(in blue) to all reviewers’ questions and comments (in black). We do hope that the
editor and reviewers may appreciate our extended efforts to improve the paper
following their suggestions, and we also hope our efforts and clarifications may
convince the reviewers of the significant advances of our proposed strategies in
providing the paradigm of chiral emission in out-of-plane mirror symmetric
metasurfaces.
In the response letter and revised manuscript, we have addressed problems mainly
in following aspects:
1. Title: Clarified the terminology by replacing “non-chiral” with “intrinsically
achiral metasurface” to avoid ambiguity.
2. Novelty: Performed a targeted comparison with representative prior works and our
group’s earlier studies across structural design, symmetry conditions, optical
response, and underlying mechanisms, thereby highlighting the distinct
contributions of this work.
3. New figure: Incorporated both simulated spectra and temporal coupled-mode
theory (TCMT) fitting curves into Figure 3, highlighting the strong agreement
between analytical TCMT predictions and numerical results. In Figure 4b,
extended the x- and y-axis ranges to better reveal the trends under larger asymmetry
parameters ( and t).
4. Supplementary information: Revised Section 3 to enhance readability and ensure
rigor in the derivation. Added Section 5 to explicitly reveal the role of symmetry
breaking perturbations via the overlap-integral formulation, supported by
additional figures.
We believe these revisions fully address the concerns regarding novelty and
provide a clearer distinction from previous works. We thank the Reviewers again for
their constructive and insightful feedback.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have addressed all of my comments and resolved the issues I previously raised. While relevant works exist in the literature, the current manuscript explored distinct aspects and reported interesting new features, particularly clarifying the role of the anisotropic continuum in vertical chiral emission. As explained in the response letter, the current manuscript presents a design principle that is broadly applicable across a wide class of chiral metasurfaces. Therefore, I believe this work will be of broad interest and is well-suited for the diverse readership of Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In my first report, I recognized the timeliness of the topic addressed in the paper but expressed serious doubts regarding the fundamental novelty of the reported results. My major concern was that the authors have already presented the very same effect – chiral emission of light – performed by practically identically designed silicon metasurface in their recent paper. In the original manuscript they managed to fully avoid mentioning this paper. Now it is cited as [12]. In addition, I formulated a couple of suggestions regarding the theoretical background and presentation in case the authors decide to publish the paper elsewhere.
In response, the authors write: “The apparent similarity in metasurface geometry is intentional and crucial to the purpose of this study. In our previous work, the metasurface was placed on a dielectric substrate that breaks out-of-plane mirror symmetry and belongs to different classifications as our current work. To isolate the impact of out-of-plane symmetry, we intentionally retained the same in-plane geometry” and also “We have no intention of repeating prior work. On the contrary, our aim is to highlight the conceptual contrast by keeping geometry constant and varying only the symmetry condition”
These rather strong statements, however, are not backed in the paper. Instead of resolving the issue, they raise even more serious concerns:
1. If the similarity to the previous work was intentional, why was it not stated anywhere in the text, and why was the relevant paper not mentioned and cited? Where in the latest version can we read about the physical consequences of the “conceptual contrast” between the previous and current metasurfaces?
2. If the presence of dielectric substrate was so crucial in the previous work, why did the authors write there that “The out-of-plane symmetry is nearly preserved in the current structure since the side wall of the silicon pillars is vertical and the symmetry breaking induced by the silica substrate is weak.” (see page 2 in Ref. 12). Note that this is a very reasonable statement. Typically, weakly refracting substrates marginally affect optical properties of silicon metasurfaces: one should really search for very specific situations, when a substrate plays a noticeable role.
3. Is there any scientific evidence of a qualitative difference in the performance of metasurfaces from the present and previous works?
4. If the out-of-plane symmetry is so crucial, to which extent should one preserve it for the reported effects to take place? Note that the latest metasurface is neither fully symmetrically fabricated. This is seen in Supplementary Fig. S9 subplot 9, as well as it is manifested by different emission spectra from both sides given in Fig. 4e).
In response to my other comments, the authors extended the discussion of how the birefringent background scattering (they call it anisotropic continuum) can be related to other low-quality-factor resonances. They reasonably note that there can be several resonances contributing here. However, then in SI they attempt to formulate a temporal coupled mode theory (TCMT) describing how the birefringent background can arise due to a single broad resonant mode. I expressed doubts that this is possible, and now would like to warn the authors that their newly added statements are most likely erroneous. Such a procedure expectedly violates the time reversal and energy conservation. This is now explicitly shown by the authors themselves as they arrive at the necessity of Supplementary Eq. (22), which requires the equality of frequency omega to the eigenfrequency omega_c. This particularly means that the time reversal is granted for monochromatic fields of one specific frequency. Of course, the fundamental physical laws must be valid in the whole frequency range where TCMT is considered applicable.
Also, in response to my suggestions, the authors have extended the paper by adding TCMT spectra to Fig. 3, and Supplementary Section 5 describing the resonant mode spatial structure and the details of its coupling to plane waves when the structure symmetry is perturbed. I truly appreciate this.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Manipulating emission polarization is crucial for advanced applications such as polarized fluorescence and lasing, thermal radiation control, stereochemistry and spintronics. Existing approaches for generating circularly polarized emission primarily rely on nanostructures with true chirality, where the far-field polarization at the Γ point is believed to require out-of-plane symmetry breaking. This raises a question: can an intrinsically achiral metasurface that preserves out-of-plane symmetry generate chiral emission? Here, we introduce the concept of anisotropic continuum, defined as a continuum state exhibiting distinct responses for orthogonal polarizations of incidence, as a new degree of freedom for intrinsically achiral metasurfaces. In such metasurfaces, chiral emission arises from manipulating the anisotropic continuum together with the metasurface’s in-plane perturbations. Degrees of circular polarization of 0.83 for upward emission and −0.9 for downward emission are achieved experimentally by integrating the fabricated silicon metasurface with fluorescent organic dyes. Our findings not only address a long-standing gap in the understanding of structural chirality, but also open new opportunities for high-performance applications in polarized fluorescence and thermal emission.

---

## Introduction

Electromagnetic chirality refers to the phenomenon in which an object interacts differently with right and left circularly polarized (RCP/LCP) light1–4, a property commonly observed in natural materials with three-dimensional asymmetric structures. This chiral behavior gives rise to a distinct chiroptical response, which can be characterized by circular dichroism (CD) or optical rotation5. While natural materials have been used to generate chiral emission, their low chirality and limited tunability constrain practical applications6,7. Metasurfaces, however, offer a powerful platform to enhance and control chiral emission, enabling new opportunities in polarized emission8–13, chirality tuning14,15, chiral sensing16,17, and photodetection18,19.

Recent advances in chiral metasurfaces and their ability to generate chiral emission have been driven by the incorporation of non-local resonances, especially bound states in the continuum (BIC)20–29 and guided modes30. In such systems, light remains confined within the metasurface while coexisting with a continuum of electromagnetic waves. Typically, intrinsic chirality in metasurfaces, characterized by chiroptical responses at the Γ point, is achieved in geometrically chiral structures through symmetry breaking across all mirror planes6,31–34. To break the out-of-plane mirror symmetry (σz symmetry) and achieve chiral quasi-BIC, various methods have been employed, including slant-etching9,24, grayscale lithography10,25 and bi-layer design35. In these structures, chiral emission arises when the quasi-BIC aligns with a high-transmission background. With mirror symmetry breaking in all planes, chiral emission occurs when near-unity CD is observed (indicated in the left panel of Fig. 1a)24,28. Here, chiral emission refers to a radiative process in which the far-field degree of circular polarization (DCP=(IR − IL)/(IR + IL)) approaches unity. Planar chiral metasurfaces represent another route, where near-unity CD29,36,37 at normal incidence has also been reported. However, these designs primarily focus on transmission properties, and their potential for controlling emission remains largely unexplored (see Supplementary Section 1). Moreover, recent studies have revealed that a large CD in transmission does not necessarily correspond to chiral emission24, highlighting a gap in understanding the emission mechanism of planar chiral systems. In our earlier work, chiral emission was observed in the presence of a dielectric substrate that perturbed σz symmetry12. Conventionally, σz-symmetric metasurfaces are believed to support only extrinsic chiral emission away from the Γ point, typically enabled by breaking in-plane inversion symmetry38–41. The far-field polarization at the Γ point, by contrast, is generally considered nearly linear due to the absence of geometric chirality21,24,28,42. An interesting question arises: can a metasurface with σz symmetry, which is intrinsically achiral, generate circular or even arbitrary polarization at the Γ point? Our answer is yes.

Here, we demonstrate theoretically and experimentally that breaking σz symmetry is not required to generate chiral emission at the Γ point, using a vertically etched silicon metasurface embedded in a uniform environment (right panel of Fig. 1a). An additional degree of freedom is introduced by leveraging anisotropic continuum, characterized by distinct responses for orthogonal polarizations in the continuum, e.g., x-polarized and y-polarized light. The term continuum refers to a range of states that are closely connected and form a smooth, uninterrupted spectrum43. In metasurfaces, the continuum is characterized by a slowly-varying reflection/transmission spectrum, induced by Fabry-Perot resonances44, Mie resonances45, high-contrast grating effects46, and other mechanisms. We show that when a bound mode is embedded within an anisotropic continuum, in-plane perturbations can induce radiative coupling. This leads to chiral emission within a specific continuum, where the radiated polarization exhibits opposite chirality in the upward and downward directions. While ultrahigh-Q modes in metasurfaces, such as quasi-BIC47,48 and leaky guided modes30,49,50, have been extensively studied and widely applied in photonics, the specific influence of the continuum on emission polarization remains largely unexplored. Related work has examined its effect on linearly polarized emission51, whereas its contribution to chiral emission remains an open and critical question. Understanding the role of these states could open new avenues for designing metasurfaces with customized polarization properties.

---

## Results

To show the importance of anisotropic continuum in realizing chiral emission in σz-symmetric metasurfaces, we decompose the far-field polarization of a resonant mode in the σz-symmetric metasurface into Cartesian components |Ex|eiθx and |Ey|eiθy. It is determined by two critical parameters: (i) the phase difference between the x- and y-components Ex and Ey, expressed as φ=θy − θx=arg(Ey/Ex) and (ii) the magnitude ratio of Ex and Ey, denoted as η=|Ey|/|Ex|. We start with a structure that exhibits no polarization conversion in either transmission or reflection between the x- and y-polarized channels to simplify the analysis. For a discrete localized state, the phase difference φ can be expressed in terms of background reflection and transmission coefficients (rx, ry, tx, ty) as follows (Supplementary Section 2)44,52

φ = arg(ry + αz ty) − arg(rx + αz tx) + nπ, (1)

where n is an integer and αz=±1 is a parity number. This equation establishes a connection between the eigenstate far-field polarization and the scattering coefficients of the continuum.

The relation between the eigenstate phase difference φ and the continuum transmission spectra in a σz-symmetric structure is conceptually demonstrated in Fig. 1b. For metasurfaces with a transmissive background or anisotropic continuum (left panels of Fig. 1b), φ is always zero and the vertically radiated polarization remains linearly polarized. For instance, metasurfaces with the unit cell composed of cylinders or circular apertures are unable to generate an arbitrary phase difference φ as they inherently satisfy arg(ry + αz ty)=arg(rx + αz tx). In contrast, a nonzero phase difference between the x- and y-components of the radiated electric field can be generated with the assistance of the anisotropic continuum (right panels of Fig. 1b). To achieve chiral emission, φ=π/2 should be satisfied first. This requires that the metasurface should generally be geometrically anisotropic in a certain direction.

Due to the presence of anisotropic continuum, the transmission and reflection spectra of σz-symmetric metasurfaces exhibit unique features compared with σz-asymmetric ones. As shown in Fig. 1c, under the condition of DCP=1, RCP incidence excites a strong resonance; however, its transmission remains identical to the non-resonant direct transmission under LCP incidence, due to destructive interference with the background (Supplementary Section 3). Consequently, the transmission CD at the Γ point ideally vanishes when the resonant and background scatterings are exactly out of phase.

We consider a σz-symmetric dielectric metasurface, schematically shown in Fig. 1d. The unit cell consists of a silicon dimer embedded in a silica environment, preserving σz symmetry regardless of in-plane variations. This adopted structure follows our earlier work to isolate and emphasize the role of out-of-plane mirror symmetry12. The phase difference φ of the structure is governed by anisotropic continuum modulation, while the ratio η=|Ey|/|Ex| is influenced by in-plane perturbations. Initially, with α=0 and δt=0, no symmetry breaking occurs, and the introduction of the continuum results in φ=π/2. In this condition, the bound mode is embedded in the continuum, allowing coupling to x-polarized waves. Further introducing nonzero α induces simultaneous non-zero |Ex| and |Ey|, producing circular polarization. In this step, breaking the in-plane mirror symmetry to make the structure “2D-chiral” is essential for generating both |Ex| and |Ey|, as the in-plane mirror symmetry guarantees linear polarization. Figure 1e provides a clearer illustration of the role of the anisotropic continuum. The polarization of the far-field radiation can be fully described by a set of Stokes parameters: S1=(|Ex|2−|Ey|2)/(|Ex|2+|Ey|2), S2=2|Ex||Ey|cosφ/(|Ex|2+|Ey|2), S3=2|Ex||Ey|sinφ/(|Ex|2+|Ey|2). Once φ is fixed, the Stokes parameters trace an arc on the Poincare sphere connecting two opposite points on the S1 axis as |Ex| and |Ey| vary. In this case, the phase difference φ is the angle between the arc and the equator, while |Ey|/|Ex| controls the distance between the observed point and the pole along the S1 axis. Without the contribution of anisotropic continuum, radiative modes induced by in-plane symmetry breaking trace a line along the equator of the Poincare sphere (gray line in Fig. 1e). When anisotropic continuum is introduced, this line is lifted toward either the northern or southern hemisphere. Under specific structural parameters, the trajectory intersects the pole, marked by a red star. This evolution is further depicted in the right panel of Fig. 1e, highlighting the changes in the radiated polarization as the structural parameters vary.

To demonstrate control over the phase difference φ, we select an unperturbed metasurface with α=0 and δt=0, and then vary the pillar length L. This variation induces anisotropy of the background response, which results in nontrivial values of φ according to Eq. (1). Note also that the phase difference φ depends on the relative positions between the bound mode and the broad transmission dip of Ty. The variation of φ with L is shown in Fig. 2a, where φ decreases with increasing L and reaches φ=π/2 when L=190 nm. The corresponding transmission spectra Tx and Ty for L=190 nm are shown in the inset of Fig. 2a, with the position of the bound mode marked as a red star. Under this condition, further modulation of the asymmetric parameters α and δt transforms the bound mode into a bright mode that radiates into the far-field. The far-field polarization distribution in k-space is shown on the right side of Fig. 2b, revealing a C point at the Γ point.

A silicon metasurface with α=0.09 and δt=11 nm is fabricated on a silica substrate to experimentally verify our theoretical predictions. The metasurface is subsequently covered with a 50 μm layer of PMMA to achieve refractive index matching with the silica substrate24 (so that the silicon metasurface is symmetrical along the vertical direction) and to minimize the impact of Fabry-Perot resonance on the spectrum. Figure 2c presents the overall scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of the silicon metasurface together with a schematic illustration in the x-z plane, revealing vertically etched structures that preserve the out-of-plane mirror symmetry. Angle-resolved transmission spectra for transverse electric (TE) and transverse magnetic (TM) polarized incident light, denoted by TTE and TTM, respectively, are confirmed by simulations and experiments in Fig. 2d. Under TM-polarized incidence, only the TM mode is excited, whereas TE-polarized incidence excites TM1, TE1, and TM2 modes (note that TE/TM incidence refers to the incident polarization, while TE/TM modes refer to the eigenmodes). The TM1 mode couples to TE and TM components, residing within the broad transmission dip observed under TE incidence. The experimental results closely align with the simulations, confirming the coupling of the TM1 mode to both the x- and y-polarization components and its modulation by the continuum. While the primary discussion in the main text focuses on the TM1 mode, the TE mode also holds potential for chiral emission, as elaborated in the Supplementary Section 4.

To investigate the evolution of radiated polarization, we fabricated a series of metasurfaces with varying configurations: zero α and δt, nonzero δt only, and both nonzero α and δt. Transmission spectra of these metasurfaces were simulated (solid lines in Fig. 3), theoretically derived with TCMT (indicated by “×” in Fig. 3), and experimentally measured (indicated by “Δ” in Fig. 3) to provide insight into the continuum and bound modes. For α=0 and δt=0, the transmission spectrum Ty exhibits a broad dip between 700 nm and 900 nm, while Tx maintains high transmission (Fig. 3a). In this configuration, no bound mode is excited due to symmetry protection. The phase difference φ is calculated through Eq. (1) with αz=−1, and is depicted as a dotted gray line in the upper panel of Fig. 3a. Although a nonzero φ is generated across the wavelength range, we have |Ex|=|Ey|=0. For α=0 and δt=11 nm, the bound TM1 mode becomes leaky, experimentally resulting in a sharp transmission dip at λ=778 nm for Tx, while the line shape of Ty remains nearly unchanged (Fig. 3b). This leakage, independent of C2 symmetry breaking, indicates that the mode is a quasi-guided mode arising from band-doubling rather than a symmetry-protected BIC. For α=0.09 and δt=11 nm, the transmission spectra exhibit resonant features under both x-polarized and y-polarized light illumination. At λ=775 nm, a transmission dip appears for Tx while a transmission peak emerges for Ty, located near the broad dip of Ty (Fig. 3c). The simultaneous presence of the dip and peak signifies coupling to both x- and y-polarizations. The TCMT-fitted spectra show excellent agreement with numerical simulations, validating that the model accurately describes the key features of vertical chiral emission.

In terms of the resonant mode field distribution, the coupling behavior can be directly understood from the overlap integral between the incident field and the resonant mode: symmetry enforces zero overlap, δt alone allows coupling only to x-polarization, and the combination of δt and α yields finite overlap for both x- and y-polarizations with a phase difference close to π/2. Full derivations and supporting figures are provided in Supplementary Section 5.

The chiral emission capabilities of metasurfaces play a significant role in modulating fluorescence, laser emission and thermal radiation. Here, we further examine the fluorescence properties enabled by the σz-symmetric dielectric metasurface, with the absorption characteristics shown in Supplementary Section 6. As shown in Fig. 4a, in the case where L=190 nm, the long and short axes of the radiated polarization consistently align with the x or y axis, with only the ellipticity changing as α and δt vary. Thus, the phase difference φ remains nearly π/2 for small values of α and δt. This variation demonstrates that the phase difference φ induced by continuum scattering coefficients is robust against in-plane perturbations. Since δt and α control |Ex| and |Ey| independently, there are multiple instances where |Ey|/|Ex|=1, resulting in C points (Fig. 4b). Larger values of α and δt introduce greater symmetry breaking, which leads to lower Q-factors. In the experiment, a thin layer of IR140 organic dye is first spin-coated onto the fabricated metasurface, followed by a 50 μm PMMA coating. The sample is then excited with a 532 nm laser, and its photoluminescence (PL) characteristics are analyzed (Supplementary Section 7). The PL from the dye is strongly modulated by the TM1 mode supported by the metasurface, with its polarization determined by the eigenstate. Figure 4c displays the polarization-resolved upward PL spectra for three cases with different α values at a fixed δt of 11 nm. For α=0, the RCP and LCP components of the PL spectrum are nearly equal, indicating linearly polarized emission. As α increases, the proportion of the LCP component decreases, resulting in an increased DCP.

Figure 4d demonstrates the x-z cross sections of Ex±iEy of the eigenstate in the case of α=0.09 and δt=11 nm. The upward and downward leaky waves are RCP (red circular line) and LCP (blue circular line), both represented by Ex − iEy due to the change in direction21. The reversal of radiated circular polarization is expected, given that the structure exhibits opposite chirality when viewed from above and below. Experimentally, a prominent RCP peak is detected in the upward emission, with negligible LCP contribution, resulting in a DCP of 0.83 (upper half of Fig. 4e). Conversely, for downward emission, the LCP component dominates, yielding a DCP of −0.9 (lower half of Fig. 4e). This reversal in circular polarization confirms the absence of net chiral flux in the far field, consistent with the preserved σz symmetry. The small difference in absolute DCP between the upward and downward emissions may be attributed to the coated thin dye layer, which degrades the out-of-plane symmetry to some extent.

---

## Methods

Numerical simulation
All simulations are performed using COMSOL Multiphysics 5.6 “Electromagnetic Waves Frequency Domain” module. The refractive indices of silicon and surrounding materials are taken as nSi=3.9 (Supplementary Section 10) and nPMMA=nSiO2=1.45, respectively. Periodic conditions are applied in the x and y directions of the simulated unit cell, and perfectly matched layers are employed along the z direction. The far-field eigen-polarization is calculated through COMSOL Multiphysics 5.6 with MATLAB. In the calculation of continuum transmission, the incidence port is set as x/y polarization by setting the electric mode field to (1, 0, 0) or (0, 1, 0). Equation (1) is calculated through the polarization-resolved scattering coefficients obtained from ports.

Sample fabrication
A layer of 210 nm silicon is deposited on a 4-inch silica substrate through plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition and subsequently cleaved into small 1 cm × 1 cm slices. You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Manipulating emission polarization is crucial for advanced applications such as polarized fluorescence and lasing, thermal radiation control, stereochemistry and spintronics. Existing approaches for generating circularly polarized emission primarily rely on nanostructures with true chirality, where the far-field polarization at the Γ point is believed to require out-of-plane symmetry breaking. This raises a question: can an intrinsically achiral metasurface that preserves out-of-plane symmetry generate chiral emission? Here, we introduce the concept of anisotropic continuum, defined as a continuum state exhibiting distinct responses for orthogonal polarizations of incidence, as a new degree of freedom for intrinsically achiral metasurfaces. In such metasurfaces, chiral emission arises from manipulating the anisotropic continuum together with the metasurface’s in-plane perturbations. Degrees of circular polarization of 0.83 for upward emission and −0.9 for downward emission are achieved experimentally by integrating the fabricated silicon metasurface with fluorescent organic dyes. Our findings not only address a long-standing gap in the understanding of structural chirality, but also open new opportunities for high-performance applications in polarized fluorescence and thermal emission.

---

## Introduction

Electromagnetic chirality refers to the phenomenon in which an object interacts differently with right and left circularly polarized (RCP/LCP) light1–4, a property commonly observed in natural materials with three-dimensional asymmetric structures. This chiral behavior gives rise to a distinct chiroptical response, which can be characterized by circular dichroism (CD) or optical rotation5. While natural materials have been used to generate chiral emission, their low chirality and limited tunability constrain practical applications6,7. Metasurfaces, however, offer a powerful platform to enhance and control chiral emission, enabling new opportunities in polarized emission8–13, chirality tuning14,15, chiral sensing16,17, and photodetection18,19.

Recent advances in chiral metasurfaces and their ability to generate chiral emission have been driven by the incorporation of non-local resonances, especially bound states in the continuum (BIC)20–29 and guided modes30. In such systems, light remains confined within the metasurface while coexisting with a continuum of electromagnetic waves. Typically, intrinsic chirality in metasurfaces, characterized by chiroptical responses at the Γ point, is achieved in geometrically chiral structures through symmetry breaking across all mirror planes6,31–34. To break the out-of-plane mirror symmetry (σz symmetry) and achieve chiral quasi-BIC, various methods have been employed, including slant-etching9,24, grayscale lithography10,25 and bi-layer design35. In these structures, chiral emission arises when the quasi-BIC aligns with a high-transmission background. With mirror symmetry breaking in all planes, chiral emission occurs when near-unity CD is observed (indicated in the left panel of Fig. 1a)24,28. Here, chiral emission refers to a radiative process in which the far-field degree of circular polarization (DCP=(IR − IL)/(IR + IL)) approaches unity. Planar chiral metasurfaces represent another route, where near-unity CD29,36,37 at normal incidence has also been reported. However, these designs primarily focus on transmission properties, and their potential for controlling emission remains largely unexplored (see Supplementary Section 1). Moreover, recent studies have revealed that a large CD in transmission does not necessarily correspond to chiral emission24, highlighting a gap in understanding the emission mechanism of planar chiral systems. In our earlier work, chiral emission was observed in the presence of a dielectric substrate that perturbed σz symmetry12. Conventionally, σz-symmetric metasurfaces are believed to support only extrinsic chiral emission away from the Γ point, typically enabled by breaking in-plane inversion symmetry38–41. The far-field polarization at the Γ point, by contrast, is generally considered nearly linear due to the absence of geometric chirality21,24,28,42. An interesting question arises: can a metasurface with σz symmetry, which is intrinsically achiral, generate circular or even arbitrary polarization at the Γ point? Our answer is yes.

Here, we demonstrate theoretically and experimentally that breaking σz symmetry is not required to generate chiral emission at the Γ point, using a vertically etched silicon metasurface embedded in a uniform environment (right panel of Fig. 1a). An additional degree of freedom is introduced by leveraging anisotropic continuum, characterized by distinct responses for orthogonal polarizations in the continuum, e.g., x-polarized and y-polarized light. The term continuum refers to a range of states that are closely connected and form a smooth, uninterrupted spectrum43. In metasurfaces, the continuum is characterized by a slowly-varying reflection/transmission spectrum, induced by Fabry-Perot resonances44, Mie resonances45, high-contrast grating effects46, and other mechanisms. We show that when a bound mode is embedded within an anisotropic continuum, in-plane perturbations can induce radiative coupling. This leads to chiral emission within a specific continuum, where the radiated polarization exhibits opposite chirality in the upward and downward directions. While ultrahigh-Q modes in metasurfaces, such as quasi-BIC47,48 and leaky guided modes30,49,50, have been extensively studied and widely applied in photonics, the specific influence of the continuum on emission polarization remains largely unexplored. Related work has examined its effect on linearly polarized emission51, whereas its contribution to chiral emission remains an open and critical question. Understanding the role of these states could open new avenues for designing metasurfaces with customized polarization properties.

---

## Results

To show the importance of anisotropic continuum in realizing chiral emission in σz-symmetric metasurfaces, we decompose the far-field polarization of a resonant mode in the σz-symmetric metasurface into Cartesian components |Ex|eiθx and |Ey|eiθy. It is determined by two critical parameters: (i) the phase difference between the x- and y-components Ex and Ey, expressed as φ=θy − θx=arg(Ey/Ex) and (ii) the magnitude ratio of Ex and Ey, denoted as η=|Ey|/|Ex|. We start with a structure that exhibits no polarization conversion in either transmission or reflection between the x- and y-polarized channels to simplify the analysis. For a discrete localized state, the phase difference φ can be expressed in terms of background reflection and transmission coefficients (rx, ry, tx, ty) as follows (Supplementary Section 2)44,52

φ = arg(ry + αz ty) − arg(rx + αz tx) + nπ, (1)

where n is an integer and αz=±1 is a parity number. This equation establishes a connection between the eigenstate far-field polarization and the scattering coefficients of the continuum.

The relation between the eigenstate phase difference φ and the continuum transmission spectra in a σz-symmetric structure is conceptually demonstrated in Fig. 1b. For metasurfaces with a transmissive background or anisotropic continuum (left panels of Fig. 1b), φ is always zero and the vertically radiated polarization remains linearly polarized. For instance, metasurfaces with the unit cell composed of cylinders or circular apertures are unable to generate an arbitrary phase difference φ as they inherently satisfy arg(ry + αz ty)=arg(rx + αz tx). In contrast, a nonzero phase difference between the x- and y-components of the radiated electric field can be generated with the assistance of the anisotropic continuum (right panels of Fig. 1b). To achieve chiral emission, φ=π/2 should be satisfied first. This requires that the metasurface should generally be geometrically anisotropic in a certain direction.

Due to the presence of anisotropic continuum, the transmission and reflection spectra of σz-symmetric metasurfaces exhibit unique features compared with σz-asymmetric ones. As shown in Fig. 1c, under the condition of DCP=1, RCP incidence excites a strong resonance; however, its transmission remains identical to the non-resonant direct transmission under LCP incidence, due to destructive interference with the background (Supplementary Section 3). Consequently, the transmission CD at the Γ point ideally vanishes when the resonant and background scatterings are exactly out of phase.

We consider a σz-symmetric dielectric metasurface, schematically shown in Fig. 1d. The unit cell consists of a silicon dimer embedded in a silica environment, preserving σz symmetry regardless of in-plane variations. This adopted structure follows our earlier work to isolate and emphasize the role of out-of-plane mirror symmetry12. The phase difference φ of the structure is governed by anisotropic continuum modulation, while the ratio η=|Ey|/|Ex| is influenced by in-plane perturbations. Initially, with α=0 and δt=0, no symmetry breaking occurs, and the introduction of the continuum results in φ=π/2. In this condition, the bound mode is embedded in the continuum, allowing coupling to x-polarized waves. Further introducing nonzero α induces simultaneous non-zero |Ex| and |Ey|, producing circular polarization. In this step, breaking the in-plane mirror symmetry to make the structure “2D-chiral” is essential for generating both |Ex| and |Ey|, as the in-plane mirror symmetry guarantees linear polarization. Figure 1e provides a clearer illustration of the role of the anisotropic continuum. The polarization of the far-field radiation can be fully described by a set of Stokes parameters: S1=(|Ex|2−|Ey|2)/(|Ex|2+|Ey|2), S2=2|Ex||Ey|cosφ/(|Ex|2+|Ey|2), S3=2|Ex||Ey|sinφ/(|Ex|2+|Ey|2). Once φ is fixed, the Stokes parameters trace an arc on the Poincare sphere connecting two opposite points on the S1 axis as |Ex| and |Ey| vary. In this case, the phase difference φ is the angle between the arc and the equator, while |Ey|/|Ex| controls the distance between the observed point and the pole along the S1 axis. Without the contribution of anisotropic continuum, radiative modes induced by in-plane symmetry breaking trace a line along the equator of the Poincare sphere (gray line in Fig. 1e). When anisotropic continuum is introduced, this line is lifted toward either the northern or southern hemisphere. Under specific structural parameters, the trajectory intersects the pole, marked by a red star. This evolution is further depicted in the right panel of Fig. 1e, highlighting the changes in the radiated polarization as the structural parameters vary.

To demonstrate control over the phase difference φ, we select an unperturbed metasurface with α=0 and δt=0, and then vary the pillar length L. This variation induces anisotropy of the background response, which results in nontrivial values of φ according to Eq. (1). Note also that the phase difference φ depends on the relative positions between the bound mode and the broad transmission dip of Ty. The variation of φ with L is shown in Fig. 2a, where φ decreases with increasing L and reaches φ=π/2 when L=190 nm. The corresponding transmission spectra Tx and Ty for L=190 nm are shown in the inset of Fig. 2a, with the position of the bound mode marked as a red star. Under this condition, further modulation of the asymmetric parameters α and δt transforms the bound mode into a bright mode that radiates into the far-field. The far-field polarization distribution in k-space is shown on the right side of Fig. 2b, revealing a C point at the Γ point.

A silicon metasurface with α=0.09 and δt=11 nm is fabricated on a silica substrate to experimentally verify our theoretical predictions. The metasurface is subsequently covered with a 50 μm layer of PMMA to achieve refractive index matching with the silica substrate24 (so that the silicon metasurface is symmetrical along the vertical direction) and to minimize the impact of Fabry-Perot resonance on the spectrum. Figure 2c presents the overall scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of the silicon metasurface together with a schematic illustration in the x-z plane, revealing vertically etched structures that preserve the out-of-plane mirror symmetry. Angle-resolved transmission spectra for transverse electric (TE) and transverse magnetic (TM) polarized incident light, denoted by TTE and TTM, respectively, are confirmed by simulations and experiments in Fig. 2d. Under TM-polarized incidence, only the TM mode is excited, whereas TE-polarized incidence excites TM1, TE1, and TM2 modes (note that TE/TM incidence refers to the incident polarization, while TE/TM modes refer to the eigenmodes). The TM1 mode couples to TE and TM components, residing within the broad transmission dip observed under TE incidence. The experimental results closely align with the simulations, confirming the coupling of the TM1 mode to both the x- and y-polarization components and its modulation by the continuum. While the primary discussion in the main text focuses on the TM1 mode, the TE mode also holds potential for chiral emission, as elaborated in the Supplementary Section 4.

To investigate the evolution of radiated polarization, we fabricated a series of metasurfaces with varying configurations: zero α and δt, nonzero δt only, and both nonzero α and δt. Transmission spectra of these metasurfaces were simulated (solid lines in Fig. 3), theoretically derived with TCMT (indicated by “×” in Fig. 3), and experimentally measured (indicated by “Δ” in Fig. 3) to provide insight into the continuum and bound modes. For α=0 and δt=0, the transmission spectrum Ty exhibits a broad dip between 700 nm and 900 nm, while Tx maintains high transmission (Fig. 3a). In this configuration, no bound mode is excited due to symmetry protection. The phase difference φ is calculated through Eq. (1) with αz=−1, and is depicted as a dotted gray line in the upper panel of Fig. 3a. Although a nonzero φ is generated across the wavelength range, we have |Ex|=|Ey|=0. For α=0 and δt=11 nm, the bound TM1 mode becomes leaky, experimentally resulting in a sharp transmission dip at λ=778 nm for Tx, while the line shape of Ty remains nearly unchanged (Fig. 3b). This leakage, independent of C2 symmetry breaking, indicates that the mode is a quasi-guided mode arising from band-doubling rather than a symmetry-protected BIC. For α=0.09 and δt=11 nm, the transmission spectra exhibit resonant features under both x-polarized and y-polarized light illumination. At λ=775 nm, a transmission dip appears for Tx while a transmission peak emerges for Ty, located near the broad dip of Ty (Fig. 3c). The simultaneous presence of the dip and peak signifies coupling to both x- and y-polarizations. The TCMT-fitted spectra show excellent agreement with numerical simulations, validating that the model accurately describes the key features of vertical chiral emission.

In terms of the resonant mode field distribution, the coupling behavior can be directly understood from the overlap integral between the incident field and the resonant mode: symmetry enforces zero overlap, δt alone allows coupling only to x-polarization, and the combination of δt and α yields finite overlap for both x- and y-polarizations with a phase difference close to π/2. Full derivations and supporting figures are provided in Supplementary Section 5.

The chiral emission capabilities of metasurfaces play a significant role in modulating fluorescence, laser emission and thermal radiation. Here, we further examine the fluorescence properties enabled by the σz-symmetric dielectric metasurface, with the absorption characteristics shown in Supplementary Section 6. As shown in Fig. 4a, in the case where L=190 nm, the long and short axes of the radiated polarization consistently align with the x or y axis, with only the ellipticity changing as α and δt vary. Thus, the phase difference φ remains nearly π/2 for small values of α and δt. This variation demonstrates that the phase difference φ induced by continuum scattering coefficients is robust against in-plane perturbations. Since δt and α control |Ex| and |Ey| independently, there are multiple instances where |Ey|/|Ex|=1, resulting in C points (Fig. 4b). Larger values of α and δt introduce greater symmetry breaking, which leads to lower Q-factors. In the experiment, a thin layer of IR140 organic dye is first spin-coated onto the fabricated metasurface, followed by a 50 μm PMMA coating. The sample is then excited with a 532 nm laser, and its photoluminescence (PL) characteristics are analyzed (Supplementary Section 7). The PL from the dye is strongly modulated by the TM1 mode supported by the metasurface, with its polarization determined by the eigenstate. Figure 4c displays the polarization-resolved upward PL spectra for three cases with different α values at a fixed δt of 11 nm. For α=0, the RCP and LCP components of the PL spectrum are nearly equal, indicating linearly polarized emission. As α increases, the proportion of the LCP component decreases, resulting in an increased DCP.

Figure 4d demonstrates the x-z cross sections of Ex±iEy of the eigenstate in the case of α=0.09 and δt=11 nm. The upward and downward leaky waves are RCP (red circular line) and LCP (blue circular line), both represented by Ex − iEy due to the change in direction21. The reversal of radiated circular polarization is expected, given that the structure exhibits opposite chirality when viewed from above and below. Experimentally, a prominent RCP peak is detected in the upward emission, with negligible LCP contribution, resulting in a DCP of 0.83 (upper half of Fig. 4e). Conversely, for downward emission, the LCP component dominates, yielding a DCP of −0.9 (lower half of Fig. 4e). This reversal in circular polarization confirms the absence of net chiral flux in the far field, consistent with the preserved σz symmetry. The small difference in absolute DCP between the upward and downward emissions may be attributed to the coated thin dye layer, which degrades the out-of-plane symmetry to some extent.

All simulations are performed using COMSOL Multiphysics 5.6 “Electromagnetic Waves Frequency Domain” module.
